entries.title: UASF
entries.body:
Acronym for "*User-Activated Soft Fork*". Describes a soft fork in Bitcoin when it is initiated and enforced by the network's users through their nodes, without depending on miners' approval. The network's nodes update their software to adopt the soft fork's new rules, come what may!

Typically used in emergencies, notably when miners are mostly opposed to adopting a soft fork, the UASF serves as a means of pressure to avoid an excessive concentration of power among miners. In practice, the UASF has even become a deterrent, brandished by node operators when miners abuse their power. However, if a UASF is actually enforced, it carries risks, notably the possibility of a blockchain split, creating a new chain that may lack economic value and security. The first formal UASF proposal came from the developer Shaolin Fry, who pushed BIP-0148 in March 2017 to pressure miners who refused to signal SegWit.

entries.title: UDP
entries.body: Communication protocol used on the Internet that allows messages (datagrams) to be sent between computers without establishing a prior connection (unlike TCP). UDP is a fast transfer method, but with no guarantee of delivery, packet ordering, or error handling. It is rather used for applications requiring fast, real-time broadcasting. This protocol had been used within the FIBRE (*Fast Internet Bitcoin Relay Engine*) project to speed up the propagation of Bitcoin blocks.

entries.title: UMBREL
entries.body:
Operating system for personal servers that allows self-hosting applications, including a Bitcoin node and a Lightning node. Umbrel offers a "*plug-and-play*" style web interface that simplifies the installation and management of a full node, without requiring advanced technical skills.

Umbrel runs on dedicated hardware (Umbrel Home, Umbrel Pro) or on any compatible computer via umbrelOS. Its app store includes dozens of self-hosted applications: Bitcoin Core, LND, Core Lightning, Nextcloud, Tailscale, Nostr relays, and others.

entries.title: UNIQUE ASSETS
entries.body: Assets issued via the Taproot Assets protocol that are indivisible and non-interchangeable. Unlike fungible assets (such as a currency), a unique asset cannot be divided into fractions, and each unit is distinct from the others. They are comparable to NFTs (*non-fungible tokens*) on other protocols. *Unique assets* can represent certificates, property titles, digital collectibles, or any item requiring individual identification on the Bitcoin blockchain.

entries.title: UNIVERSE
entries.body: Data repository serving as a registry for Taproot Assets assets. A *universe* stores and distributes the metadata, proofs, and provenance history of assets issued on Bitcoin via the Taproot Assets protocol. Holders and potential acquirers of assets consult a *universe* to verify the authenticity and validity of assets before accepting them. Each asset issuer can maintain its own *universe*, and these repositories can be synchronized with one another to ensure wide dissemination of the information.

entries.title: UNIX
entries.body: Family of multitasking operating systems developed starting in 1969 by Bell Labs. Designed to be simple, flexible, and portable, UNIX has influenced many modern systems. Its fundamental principles include a hierarchical file structure, the use of shell scripts, and modular utilities. UNIX is the origin of many variants, including Linux, and remains a reference in terms of stability and performance.

entries.title: UPRV
entries.body: Extended private key prefix for Nested SegWit accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

entries.title: UPUB
entries.body: Extended public key prefix for Nested SegWit accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

entries.title: URI
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Uniform Resource Identifier*". It is a standardized character string format used to identify a resource on the Internet. A URI can be either a URL (*Uniform Resource Locator*), which provides a means of accessing a resource by indicating its location on a computer network, or a URN (*Uniform Resource Name*), which names the resource without indicating how to locate it. URIs are important in the operation of the *World Wide Web*, as they allow access to resources such as web pages, documents, and services.

In the context of Bitcoin, a URI is used specifically to facilitate transactions. It allows encoding a receiving address, as well as other transaction parameters such as the amount, in a standardized format according to BIP-0021. This simplifies the payment process by allowing users to click on a link or scan a QR code, which automatically feeds the necessary information into their Bitcoin wallet application.

entries.title: UTREEXO
UTXO
entries.body: Acronym for *Unspent Transaction Output*. A UTXO is a transaction output that has not yet been spent, that is, used as an input for a new transaction. UTXOs represent the fraction of bitcoins that a user owns and that are currently available to be spent. Each UTXO is associated with a specific output script (`scriptPubKey`), which defines the conditions required to spend the bitcoins. Transactions in Bitcoin consume these UTXOs as inputs and create new UTXOs as outputs. The UTXO model is fundamental to Bitcoin, because it makes it easy to verify that transactions are not trying to spend bitcoins that do not exist or that have already been spent.

entries.title: UTXO SET
entries.body:
Refers to the set of all existing UTXOs at a given moment. In other words, it is a big list of all the different pieces of bitcoins waiting to be spent. If you add up the amounts of all the UTXOs in the UTXO set, you get the total money supply of bitcoins in circulation. Each node of the Bitcoin network maintains its own UTXO set in real time. It updates it as new valid blocks are confirmed, with the transactions they include, which consume certain UTXOs from the UTXO set, and create new ones in return.

This UTXO set is kept by each node in order to quickly verify whether the UTXOs spent in transactions are indeed legitimate. This allows them to detect and reject double-spend attempts. The UTXO set is often at the heart of concerns about Bitcoin's decentralization, because its size naturally grows very quickly. Since part of it must be kept in RAM in order to verify transactions in a reasonable time, it is possible that the UTXO set will gradually make running a full node too costly. The UTXO set also has a strong impact on the IBD (*Initial Block Download*). The larger the share of the UTXO set that can be held in RAM, the faster the IBD. On Bitcoin Core, the UTXO set is stored in the folder named `/chainstate`.
